author: Blindspot Lab team (synthetic demonstration unit; instructor-reviewable, not externally validated)
note: Each item lists source_anchors: verbatim phrases that must be found in the ingested course sources for the item to pass verification. Items with purpose 'heldout' are reserved for evaluation post-tests and are never served in practice.

items.stem: Which formula defines the conversion rate?
items.explanation: The conversion rate is the share of visitors who complete the desired action: conversions divided by visitors.
source_anchors: Conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors

items.stem: In Table 1.1 (Northwind Outdoor Co.), which channel produced the most conversions?

options.text: Email, because it has the highest conversion rate
Social, because it has the most visitors

items.explanation: Paid search produced 500 conversions (20,000 visitors × 2.5%). Email has the highest rate but only 200 conversions.

items.stem: A conversion rate rises from 2% to 3%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It rose by 1 percentage point, which is a 50% increase

items.explanation: The percentage-point change is 3 − 2 = 1 point; relative to the starting 2%, that is a 50% increase.
source_anchors: has increased by 1 percentage point

misconception_signatures.label: Reports the percent change as percentage points

items.stem: Explain why a landing page with a higher conversion rate might still produce fewer customers than another page.

key_points.text: The number of customers equals the number of visitors multiplied by the conversion rate.
A page with many more visitors can produce more customers even with a lower conversion rate.

items.explanation: Customers = visitors × conversion rate. A high rate applied to few visitors can produce fewer customers than a low rate applied to many visitors (e.g. 8% of 500 = 40 versus 3% of 4,000 = 120).
source_anchors: A high conversion rate does not guarantee a large number of conversions

items.stem: A landing page converts 2.5% of 6,000 visitors. How many customers does it produce?
items.explanation: Customers = visitors × conversion rate = 6,000 × 2.5% = 150.
source_anchors: Conversion rate = conversions ÷ visitors

items.stem: What is contribution margin per unit?

options.text: Selling price minus variable cost per unit
Selling price minus average total cost per unit, including rent

items.explanation: Contribution margin per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit; it is what each unit contributes towards fixed costs and then profit.
source_anchors: Contribution margin per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit

misconception_signatures.label: Uses average total cost instead of variable cost
Treats revenue minus ad spend as the margin

items.stem: A product's price is cut while its variable cost per unit stays the same. What happens to contribution per unit?

options.text: It falls by the full amount of the price cut
It falls by the same percentage as the price
It stays the same, because the variable cost is unchanged
It rises, because more units will sell

items.explanation: Because variable costs stay the same, the contribution per unit falls by the full amount of the price cut, which is a larger percentage fall than the price itself.
source_anchors: the contribution per unit falls by the full amount of the price cut

misconception_signatures.label: Assumes contribution moves in proportion to price (revenue logic)

items.stem: Why can a plan that 'makes up the revenue' after a price cut still leave the business worse off?

options.text: Revenue preservation ignores variable costs, so total contribution can still fall
Revenue always falls after a price cut
Fixed costs rise whenever prices fall
It cannot: preserving revenue also preserves profit

items.explanation: Keeping revenue constant needs far less extra volume than keeping contribution constant, because revenue preservation ignores variable costs.
source_anchors: Revenue preservation ignores variable costs

misconception_signatures.label: Equates revenue preservation with profit preservation

items.stem: Explain the difference between preserving revenue and preserving contribution after a price cut.

key_points.text: Preserving revenue keeps price multiplied by units constant.
Preserving contribution keeps (price minus variable cost) multiplied by units constant.
Because the variable cost does not fall, contribution per unit falls by the whole price cut, so a larger volume increase is needed to preserve contribution.

items.explanation: Revenue preservation targets price × units; contribution preservation targets (price − variable cost) × units. Since variable cost per unit does not fall, contribution preservation needs a much larger volume increase.
source_anchors: Preserving revenue and preserving contribution are different goals

items.stem: A workshop with spare capacity has a variable cost of ₹300 and an average total cost of ₹380 per unit. A one-off order offers ₹340 per unit. Which cost should the offer be compared with?

options.text: ₹300, the marginal (variable) cost, because fixed costs are paid anyway
₹380, because every unit must cover its share of rent

items.explanation: For a one-off decision with spare capacity, the relevant cost is the marginal (incremental) cost; the order adds (340 − 300) × units of contribution.
source_anchors: what matters is the marginal (incremental) cost of serving it

misconception_signatures.label: Uses average total cost for an incremental decision

items.stem: Which formula gives break-even volume?

options.text: Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit
Variable cost ÷ contribution margin per unit

items.explanation: Break-even volume is the number of units at which total contribution covers fixed costs: fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit.
source_anchors: Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit

items.stem: How is return on advertising spend (ROAS) calculated?
items.explanation: ROAS divides the revenue attributed to advertising by the advertising cost.
source_anchors: ROAS = attributed revenue ÷ advertising spend

items.stem: A business has a 40% contribution margin ratio. What is its break-even ROAS?
items.explanation: Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin ratio = 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5.
source_anchors: needs a ROAS of at least 2.5 before advertising contributes anything towards fixed costs

misconception_signatures.label: Assumes a ROAS of 1 is break-even

items.stem: In Figure 3.1, which channels had a ROAS above 1 but still lost money after advertising?

options.text: None: every channel with a ROAS above 1 made money

items.explanation: Social (ROAS 2.0x) and Display (1.5x) are above 1 but below the 2.5x break-even ROAS, so their contribution after ad spend is negative (−₹16k and −₹20k).
source_anchors: Figure 3.1 ROAS and contribution after advertising by channel

items.stem: Explain why a ROAS above 1 does not necessarily mean a campaign is profitable.

key_points.text: ROAS compares revenue, not profit, with advertising spend.
The revenue must also pay for the variable costs of the products sold.
The break-even ROAS is 1 divided by the contribution margin ratio, which is above 1.

items.explanation: ROAS uses revenue. Revenue still has to cover variable costs, so a campaign only covers its ad spend when ROAS exceeds 1 ÷ contribution margin ratio.
source_anchors: a ROAS above 1 does not mean the campaign made money

items.stem: Why can ROAS overstate the effect of a campaign?

options.text: Some attributed sales would have happened without the advertising
ROAS includes fixed costs in the denominator
ROAS is always calculated on profit rather than revenue

items.explanation: Attribution can credit sales that would have happened anyway; incrementality tests compare exposed and unexposed groups to estimate the causal effect.
source_anchors: Some attributed sales would have happened without the advertising

items.stem: According to the break-even ROAS table in the slide deck, which break-even ROAS corresponds to a 25% contribution margin ratio?
items.explanation: Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.0x, as listed in the slide table.

items.stem: How is customer acquisition cost (CAC) calculated?

options.text: Sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired

items.explanation: CAC is the total sales and marketing spend in a period divided by the number of new customers acquired in that period.
source_anchors: CAC = sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired

items.stem: Why should customer lifetime value be based on contribution rather than revenue?

options.text: Revenue ignores the cost of serving the customer, so it overstates CLV
Contribution is always larger than revenue
Revenue cannot be measured per customer
It makes no difference to decisions

items.explanation: Using revenue instead of contribution overstates CLV because it ignores the cost of serving the customer.
source_anchors: Using revenue instead of contribution overstates CLV

items.stem: Is a low customer acquisition cost always good?

options.text: Yes, cheaper acquisition is always better
No: cheap customers who churn quickly can be worth less than more expensive customers who stay
Yes, as long as ROAS is above 1

items.explanation: A low CAC is not automatically good; CAC must be compared with contribution-based lifetime value.
source_anchors: A low CAC is not automatically good

items.stem: A subscription box customer pays ₹600 a month at a 30% contribution margin ratio, and the CAC is ₹720. What is the payback period in months?
items.explanation: Monthly contribution = ₹600 × 30% = ₹180; payback = ₹720 ÷ ₹180 = 4 months.
source_anchors: With a CAC of ₹720 the payback period is four months

misconception_signatures.label: Divides CAC by revenue instead of contribution

items.stem: Which formula gives the payback period for customer acquisition?
items.explanation: Payback (months) = CAC ÷ monthly contribution per customer.
source_anchors: Payback period (months) = CAC ÷ monthly contribution per customer

items.stem: What is a confounder?

options.text: A variable that influences both a supposed cause and its effect
The treatment given in an experiment
Any variable that is correlated with revenue

items.explanation: A confounder influences both the supposed cause and its effect, creating a correlation without a causal link.
source_anchors: a variable that influences both a supposed cause and its effect

items.stem: Customers who use a loyalty app spend more than other customers. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: The app causes customers to spend more
App users spend more, but loyal high spenders may be more likely to install the app, so this alone does not show causation
It proves that spending causes app installs

items.explanation: Correlation alone does not show causation; loyal, high-spending customers may simply be more likely to install the app (a confounder).
source_anchors: Correlation alone does not show that one causes the other

items.stem: Why does random assignment in an A/B test help estimate causal effects?

options.text: It balances confounders across the groups on average
It removes the need for a control group

items.explanation: Random assignment balances confounders on average, so differences between groups can be attributed to the treatment within sampling error.
source_anchors: so that confounders are balanced on average

items.stem: With a very large sample, a 0.1 percentage-point lift in conversion is statistically significant. What follows?

options.text: Whether it is worth acting on depends on the size of the effect compared with the costs and risks
The test must have been flawed
Significance means the effect is large

items.explanation: Statistical significance says the effect is unlikely to be zero; practical significance asks whether its size justifies the cost of acting.
source_anchors: Practical significance asks whether the size of the effect is worth acting on

items.stem: Explain the difference between statistical significance and practical significance.

key_points.text: A statistically significant result would be unlikely if there were truly no effect.
Practical significance asks whether the size of the effect is large enough to be worth acting on, given costs and risks.

items.explanation: Significance concerns whether an effect is distinguishable from zero; practical significance concerns whether the effect is big enough to justify action.
source_anchors: A statistically significant result is one that would be unlikely if there were truly no effect

items.stem: In the synthetic loyalty-app test described in the slide notes, roughly what lift did the promoted group show over the holdout group?
items.explanation: The promoted group spent ₹2,050 per month versus ₹1,950 for the holdout group, a lift of about 5%.
source_anchors: a lift of about 5 percent

items.stem: What does sensitivity analysis do?

options.text: Changes one assumption at a time to see how much the result moves
Changes several assumptions together to describe pessimistic and optimistic cases
Tests whether a correlation is causal

items.explanation: Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time; scenario analysis changes several together.
source_anchors: Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time

items.stem: Five orders were worth ₹800, ₹900, ₹1,000, ₹1,100 and ₹9,200. Which value best describes a typical order?
items.explanation: The median (₹1,000) describes a typical order; the mean (₹2,600) is pulled up by the single large order.
source_anchors: the mean is ₹2,600 but the median is ₹1,000

misconception_signatures.label: Uses the mean as typical for skewed data

items.stem: When is the mean more useful than the median?

options.text: When you need totals, because the mean multiplied by the count gives the total
Never; the median is always better

items.explanation: Use the median to describe a typical customer and the mean when you need totals (mean × count = total).
source_anchors: the mean when you need totals

misconception_signatures.label: Prefers the mean for skewed data

items.stem: In Table 6.1, what is the contribution after ad spend in the expected scenario?
items.explanation: Expected case: 50,000 × 2% = 1,000 orders × ₹2,000 = ₹2,000,000 revenue × 40% = ₹800,000 contribution − ₹100,000 ad spend = ₹700,000.
source_anchors: Table 6.1 Campaign scenarios

items.stem: Explain why scenario analysis is useful when planning a campaign.

key_points.text: Business cases depend on uncertain assumptions such as conversion rate, order value and margin.
Scenario analysis changes several assumptions together to show pessimistic, expected and optimistic outcomes.

items.explanation: Results depend on assumptions; scenario analysis changes several of them together to show a range of outcomes (pessimistic, expected, optimistic).
source_anchors: Scenario analysis changes several assumptions together
